title: Bad Bunny Trademarks His Birth Name — Is a Fashion Line or a New Era Coming?
summary:
Bad Bunny is no stranger to making a statement, and his appearance at the 2026 Met Gala was no exception. The Puerto Rican superstar arrived in elaborate aged makeup, embodying the "Aging Body" theme as a dapper abuelo. But sharp-eyed fans noticed something beyond the prosthetics: a new logo emblazoned on his director's chair and the tag of his custom Zara tuxedo. It read "Benito Antonio" in a bubbly font — his birth name.

Records show that Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio, identified in filings as "AKA Bad Bunny," applied to trademark "Benito Antonio" in January 2026. While the trademark hasn't been finalized, the move aligns with the logo debut. The application was filed under a clothing class, listing items like ties, belts, and leather belts — not typical concert merch like t-shirts or hats. This has fueled speculation that the artist is venturing into fashion with his own line.

Fans are divided. Some believe this signals a retirement of the "Bad Bunny" moniker in favor of his real name, perhaps marking a more personal musical era. Others see it as a branding play tied to his ongoing "Debí Tirar Más Fotos" world tour. But the specific clothing items in the filing suggest something more entrepreneurial. Bad Bunny has a history of fashion collaborations, most recently with Zara for his Super Bowl halftime show outfit — a cream jersey paying tribute to his late uncle. A namesake clothing line would be a natural extension, blending his heritage with his evolving artistic identity. For now, the conejo remains mysterious, but one thing is clear: Benito Antonio is a name to watch.
why_it_matters: Bad Bunny’s trademark move illustrates how today’s artists are not just musicians but entrepreneurs building personal brands. For teenagers growing up in a creator economy, it's a real-world lesson in intellectual property and how to leverage fame into fashion—and maybe a whole new career direction.

background_read: Bad Bunny, born Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio in Vega Baja, Puerto Rico, rose to global fame in the late 2010s as a reggaeton and Latin trap artist, becoming one of the world’s most-streamed musicians.

The Met Gala, held annually on the first Monday in May, is organized by Vogue editor Anna Wintour and marks the opening of the Costume Institute’s fashion exhibit; its guest list and avant-garde outfits generate massive media attention.
He has previously ventured into fashion with collaborations for Adidas, Crocs, and Gucci, as well as the custom Zara tuxedo for the Met Gala that featured the new logo.
His most recent Super Bowl halftime show appearance came in 2025 when he performed with a cream jersey that paid homage to his late uncle—an outfit made in partnership with Zara.
Many musicians have turned their personal names into clothing lines, most famously Rihanna's Fenty brand with LVMH, showing how pop stardom can launch a luxury fashion empire.

perspectives.description: A clothing line under his birth name could celebrate Bad Bunny's Puerto Rican roots and allow fans to connect with his heritage in a personal way. It also opens a creative outlet beyond music.

Some critics might view this as a cash grab, especially if it signals less focus on music. Fans who cherish the rebellious 'Bad Bunny' persona could feel alienated if he drops the stage name and becomes a luxury brand.

This fits a broader pattern where musicians—like Rihanna, Kanye West, and Pharrell—use their celebrity to enter the fashion industry. Trademarking a personal name is often a legal first step to protect a future brand, regardless of how it's used later.

If the trademark is finalized and a fashion line launches, 'Benito Antonio' could become a global label while Bad Bunny continues to release music under either name. The next tour or album might weave fashion and music together even more directly, setting a new template for Latin artists.
